---
title: Subscribers
---

A subscriber is a person: an email address, an optional name, a global status, a bag of custom attributes, and the lists they are on. Almost everything your app does with Listmonk starts here.

## Creating one

```python
sub = listmonk.create_subscriber(
    'jane@example.com',
    'Jane Doe',
    list_ids={1, 7},
    pre_confirm=True,
    attribs={'plan': 'pro', 'signup_source': 'webinar'},
)
print(sub.id, sub.uuid)
```

[`create_subscriber()`](../reference/create_subscriber.qmd) lowercases and strips the email, strips the name, and always creates the person with a global status of `enabled`. The `list_ids` set is optional. `pre_confirm=True` tells Listmonk that your app already obtained consent, so it marks the subscriptions confirmed and sends no double opt-in email; leave it off for a double opt-in list and Listmonk will ask the person to confirm. `attribs` is any JSON-serialisable dict and is stored as-is.

If the email already exists, Listmonk answers 409 and the client raises `httpx2.HTTPStatusError`. Look the person up first when that is a possibility; the [signup recipe](recipes.qmd#handle-a-signup-form) does exactly that.

## Finding one

```python
by_email = listmonk.subscriber_by_email('jane@example.com')
by_id = listmonk.subscriber_by_id(201)
by_uuid = listmonk.subscriber_by_uuid('c37786af-e6ab-4260-9b49-740a8cd6a7ed')
```

All three return a [`Subscriber`](../reference/models.Subscriber.qmd) or `None`. They never raise just because nobody matched.

Two of them have a permission requirement worth knowing about. [`subscriber_by_email()`](../reference/subscriber_by_email.qmd) and [`subscriber_by_uuid()`](../reference/subscriber_by_uuid.qmd) send a server-side SQL filter, so the API user's role needs `subscribers:sql_query` or the server answers 403. [`subscriber_by_id()`](../reference/subscriber_by_id.qmd) uses Listmonk's direct per-subscriber endpoint and needs only ordinary read permission. The value you pass to the email and UUID lookups is sent as a quoted SQL literal with embedded quotes escaped, so user-supplied input cannot widen the match.

## Finding many

```python
on_the_list = listmonk.subscribers(list_id=7)
in_portland = listmonk.subscribers(query_text="subscribers.attribs->>'city' = 'Portland'")
both = listmonk.subscribers(query_text="subscribers.status = 'enabled'", list_id=7)
```

[`subscribers()`](../reference/subscribers.qmd) fetches every match, 500 per page, and joins the pages, ordered by `updated_at` descending. With no arguments it returns the whole instance, so give it a long `timeout_config` on a big one. The `query_text` is Listmonk's SQL-like filter over the `subscribers` table; custom attributes live in a JSONB column and are reached with `->>`. The [Listmonk querying docs](https://listmonk.app/docs/querying-and-segmentation/) cover the syntax. Filtering by `list_id` alone needs no special permission; passing `query_text` needs `subscribers:sql_query`.

Values you interpolate into `query_text` yourself are your responsibility. Quote them as SQL literals and never splice raw user input into the filter.

## Changing one

Updates follow one pattern across the whole library: fetch the model, change what you like, pass it back. The client sends the whole record to the server and returns the server's fresh copy.

```python
sub = listmonk.subscriber_by_email('jane@example.com')
sub.name = 'Jane A. Doe'
sub.attribs['plan'] = 'enterprise'
sub = listmonk.update_subscriber(sub, add_to_lists={4}, remove_from_lists={7})
```

[`update_subscriber()`](../reference/update_subscriber.qmd) works out list membership as "the lists she is on now, minus `remove_from_lists`, plus `add_to_lists`", and marks those subscriptions confirmed. Her global status is kept as it is unless you pass `status=`, so changing a blocklisted person's name does not put them back on your lists. The return value is the subscriber re-fetched from the server, or `None` in the unlikely case that the re-fetch finds nothing.

Because the whole record is sent, two callers updating the same subscriber at the same time will overwrite each other. Fetch, change, and update in one short sequence.

## Pausing, unsubscribing, and deleting

People pause, people leave, and sometimes people ask to be forgotten. Those are three different operations.

```python
sub = listmonk.disable_subscriber(sub)   # status 'disabled': delivery paused, reversible
sub = listmonk.enable_subscriber(sub)    # status 'enabled': back on

sub = listmonk.block_subscriber(sub)     # status 'blocklisted': the real unsubscribe

listmonk.delete_subscriber('jane@example.com')            # gone, by email
listmonk.delete_subscriber(overriding_subscriber_id=201)  # gone, by ID, no lookup first
```

[`disable_subscriber()`](../reference/disable_subscriber.qmd) and [`enable_subscriber()`](../reference/enable_subscriber.qmd) toggle delivery without touching anything else. [`block_subscriber()`](../reference/block_subscriber.qmd) is the proper unsubscribe: the record stays, so a later import cannot accidentally resurrect the person, but nothing is sent to them again. [`delete_subscriber()`](../reference/delete_subscriber.qmd) removes the record entirely and returns `False` if the email matched nobody.

If you only want to take someone off one list while leaving the others alone, that is not a status change at all; use `update_subscriber(sub, remove_from_lists={list_id})`. The [unsubscribe recipe](recipes.qmd#handle-an-unsubscribe-link) shows both paths side by side.

## Reading the model

A [`Subscriber`](../reference/models.Subscriber.qmd) carries `id`, `uuid`, `email`, `name`, `status`, `attribs`, `created_at`, `updated_at`, and `lists`. The `lists` field is a list of dicts straight from the server, each with the list `id`, `name`, and the `subscription_status` (`confirmed`, `unconfirmed`, or `unsubscribed`) for that membership. Calling `model_dump()` on a subscriber reduces `lists` to plain IDs and formats the timestamps the way the API expects, which is what `update_subscriber()` relies on.
